claim: Videocystometry combines intravesical pressure measurements with X-ray-based fluoroscopy of the lower urinary tract.
source: We recently developed videocystometry in rodents, which combines intravesical pressure measurements with X-ray-based fluoroscopy of the LUT, allowing the in vivo analysis of the process of urine storage and voiding with unprecedented detail.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the videocystometry technique.

claim: A neural network can be trained to automatically detect the bladder in fluoroscopic images.
source: To overcome this limitation, we developed a machine-learning method, in which we trained a neural network to automatically detect the bladder in fluoroscopic images, allowing the automatic analysis of bladder filling and voiding cycles based on large sets of time-lapse fluoroscopic images (>3 hr at 30 images/s) from behaving mice and in a noninvasive manner.
evidence: The abstract describes the development and application of the machine learning method with specific technical parameters.

claim: Urethane has a profound, dose-dependent effect on urethral relaxation and voiding duration.
source: With this approach, we found that urethane, an injectable anesthetic that is commonly used in preclinical urological research, has a profound, dose-dependent effect on urethral relaxation and voiding duration.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract as a result of the study.

claim: Bladder capacity was decreased approximately fourfold when cystometry was performed acutely after surgical implantation of a suprapubic catheter in both awake and anesthetized mice.
source: Moreover, both in awake and in anesthetized mice, the bladder capacity was decreased ~fourfold when cystometry was performed acutely after surgical implantation of a suprapubic catheter.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the study comparing catheterized and non-catheterized conditions.

claim: An estimated 20% of the population suffers from some sort of lower urinary tract dysfunction.
source: An estimated 20% of the population suffers from some sort of lower urinary tract dysfunction (LUTd), such as urinary incontinence, frequency, urgency, or bladder pain, which can have a strongly negative impact on health and wellbeing.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the introduction, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: Mice are favored models in preclinical lower urinary tract research due to their anatomical and physiological similarities to humans, cost-effectiveness, and availability of genetically modified strains.
source: Due to their anatomical and physiological similarities to humans, their cost-effectiveness, and the availability of a vast number of genetically modified strains, mice are favored models in preclinical LUT research (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ito et al., 2017.

claim: Cystometry has been considered the gold standard technique to study bladder function in mice in vivo in the last decades.
source: In the last decades, cystometry has been considered the gold standard technique to study bladder function in mice in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cystometry is an experimental procedure whereby the bladder is continuously filled via an implanted catheter and pressure inside the bladder is monitored during multiple filling and voiding cycles.
source: Cystometry is an experimental procedure whereby the bladder is continuously filled via an implanted catheter, and pressure inside the bladder is monitored during multiple filling and voiding cycles.
evidence: This is a definitional statement describing the cystometry technique.

claim: Urethral electromyography has been used to complement cystometry to provide simultaneous information regarding the activity of the urethral sphincters.
source: More recently, this technique has sometimes been complemented with urethral electromyography (UEM) to provide simultaneous information regarding the activity of the urethral sphincters (Kadekawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kadekawa et al., 2016.

claim: Cystometry and urethral electromyography do not provide quantitative information regarding the filling state of the bladder or the urethral flow.
source: First, cystometry and UEM do not provide quantitative information regarding the filling state of the bladder or the urethral flow, whereas changes in these parameters are hallmarks of various LUTds.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing techniques.

claim: Cystometry and urethral electromyography require the introduction of a catheter in the bladder wall and metal electrodes in the urethral sphincter, both of which can affect lower urinary tract function.
source: Second, cystometry and UEM require the introduction of, respectively, a catheter in the bladder wall and metal electrodes in the urethral sphincter, both of which can affect LUT function.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation with potential functional consequences.

claim: Cystometry and urethral electromyography are mostly performed on urethane anesthetized or physically restrained mice.
source: Third, cystometry and UEM are mostly performed on urethane anesthetized or physically restrained mice to avoid complications and artifacts due to animal movement.
evidence: This describes common practice in the field.

claim: The consequences of cystometry and urethral electromyography procedures on lower urinary tract function in mice are incompletely understood.
source: The consequences of these procedures on LUT function in mice are incompletely understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Videocystometry provides quantitative and time-resolved measurements of bladder volume and urethral flow.
source: By imaging the contrast-filled bladder at video rate, this approach provides quantitative and time-resolved measurements of bladder volume and urethral flow, along with other relevant aspects of LUT function such as vesicoureteral reflux and micromotions of the bladder wall (Franken et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franken et al., 2021.

claim: Videocystometry allows measurement of vesicoureteral reflux and micromotions of the bladder wall.
source: By imaging the contrast-filled bladder at video rate, this approach provides quantitative and time-resolved measurements of bladder volume and urethral flow, along with other relevant aspects of LUT function such as vesicoureteral reflux and micromotions of the bladder wall (Franken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a capability of videocystometry with citation support.

claim: Accurate analysis of bladder volume and urethral flow during consecutive filling-voiding cycles relies on the precise delineation of the bladder.
source: Notably, the accurate analysis of bladder volume and urethral flow during consecutive filling–voiding cycles relies on the precise delineation of the bladder.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological requirement.

claim: Precise bladder delineation is readily achieved in anesthetized or otherwise motion-restrained mice where the constant background of fluoroscopic images can be subtracted.
source: This is readily achieved in anesthetized or otherwise motion-restrained mice, where the constant background of fluoroscopic images can be subtracted.
evidence: This describes a methodological capability under specific conditions.

claim: In awake, unrestrained, and behaving animals, the position of the bladder relative to other structures visible in fluoroscopic images changes constantly.
source: However, in awake, unrestrained, and behaving animals, the position of the bladder relative to other structures visible in the fluoroscopic images (e.g., bones) changes constantly.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the challenge in awake animals.

claim: Manual tracking of the bladder border is feasible for a limited number of fluoroscopic images but unworkable for typical minutes-to-hours-long imaging sessions at 30 images/s yielding >10^5 images.
source: Therefore, our earlier analyses relied on manual tracking of the border of the bladder, which is feasible for a limited number of fluoroscopic images but clearly unworkable for typical minutes-to-hours-long imaging sessions at 30 images/s, yielding >105 images.
evidence: This describes a practical limitation of manual analysis.

claim: The machine-learning protocol successfully identified the bladder border compared to manual bladder wall delineation in time-lapse image sequences, irrespective of the posture of the animal or phase of the filling/voiding cycle.
source: The machine-learning protocol was able successfully identify the bladder border compared to manual bladder wall delineation in time-lapse image sequences, irrespective of the posture of the animal or phase of the filling/voiding cycle (Figure 1B–C; Figure 1—video 1, and Figure 1—video 2), with the exception of brief failures of one or two frames during abrupt mouse movements or when the bladder was almost fully emptied.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in figures and videos.

claim: The machine-learning protocol had brief failures of one or two frames during abrupt mouse movements or when the bladder was almost fully emptied.
source: The machine-learning protocol was able successfully identify the bladder border compared to manual bladder wall delineation in time-lapse image sequences, irrespective of the posture of the animal or phase of the filling/voiding cycle (Figure 1B–C; Figure 1—video 1, and Figure 1—video 2), with the exception of brief failures of one or two frames during abrupt mouse movements or when the bladder was almost fully emptied.
evidence: This describes limitations of the method observed in the data.

claim: During efficient voids, the lowest volume at which the bladder was successfully detected by the machine-learning protocol was 4.1 ± 2.2 µl (n = 15 voids from 3 animals).
source: During efficient voids, the lowest volume at which the bladder was successfully detected by the machine-learning protocol was 4.1 ± 2.2 µl (n = 15 voids from 3 animals).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: The median Dice similarity index value was 0.95 (mean ± standard deviation: 0.92 ± 0.13), indicating overall excellent agreement between human annotation and network prediction.
source: This analysis yielded a median DISI value of 0.95 (mean ± standard deviation [SD]: 0.92 ± 0.13), indicating overall excellent agreement between human annotation and network prediction.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of the neural network performance.

claim: Urethane is the most predominantly used anesthetic during in vivo cystometry in rodents.
source: Next, we used this approach to evaluate the dose-dependent effects of urethane, the most predominantly used anesthetic during in vivo cystometry in rodents, on LUT function.
evidence: This is stated as established practice in the field.

claim: Urethane was administered at four time points, leading to a stepwise increase of the total dose from 0 to 1.2 g/kg bodyweight.
source: Urethane was administered at four time points, leading to a stepwise increase of the total dose from 0 to 1.2 g/kg bodyweight, the latter being the typical dose used in most rodent studies.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: 1.2 g/kg bodyweight is the typical dose of urethane used in most rodent studies.
source: Urethane was administered at four time points, leading to a stepwise increase of the total dose from 0 to 1.2 g/kg bodyweight, the latter being the typical dose used in most rodent studies.
evidence: This is stated as common practice in the field.

claim: Urethane did not have a statistically significant effect on bladder capacity.
source: Urethane did not have a statistically significant effect on BC (Figure 2C), but exhibited a pronounced and dose-dependent effect on RV and Evoiding (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Urethane exhibited a pronounced and dose-dependent effect on residual volume and voiding efficiency.
source: Urethane did not have a statistically significant effect on BC (Figure 2C), but exhibited a pronounced and dose-dependent effect on RV and Evoiding (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: Awake animals completely emptied their bladder at each void.
source: Indeed, whereas awake animals completely emptied their bladder at each void, urethane at doses >0.3 g/kg caused a dose-dependent increase in the volume that remained after each void and a corresponding decrease in Evoiding from ~100% to below 50% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from the study data.

claim: Urethane at doses >0.3 g/kg caused a dose-dependent increase in the volume that remained after each void and a corresponding decrease in voiding efficiency from approximately 100% to below 50%.
source: Indeed, whereas awake animals completely emptied their bladder at each void, urethane at doses >0.3 g/kg caused a dose-dependent increase in the volume that remained after each void and a corresponding decrease in Evoiding from ~100% to below 50% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The intercontractile interval decreased concomitantly with the reduced efficiency of voiding.
source: The intercontractile interval (ICI) decreased concomitantly with the reduced efficiency of voiding (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Animals that were immediately treated with a single 1.2 g/kg dose yielded similar values for bladder capacity, residual volume, and voiding efficiency as animals that reached this dose at the end of the stepwise dosing protocol.
source: Note that animals that were immediately treated with a single 1.2 g/kg-dose yielded similar values for BC, RV, and Evoiding as animals that reached this dose at the end of the stepwise dosing protocol, indicating that the reduced voiding efficiency and increased RV are due to the urethane rather than to fatigue (Figure 2C–F, blue) (Franken et al., 2021).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-F and cited work.

claim: The reduced voiding efficiency and increased residual volume are due to urethane rather than to fatigue.
source: Note that animals that were immediately treated with a single 1.2 g/kg-dose yielded similar values for BC, RV, and Evoiding as animals that reached this dose at the end of the stepwise dosing protocol, indicating that the reduced voiding efficiency and increased RV are due to the urethane rather than to fatigue (Figure 2C–F, blue) (Franken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of different dosing protocols.

claim: Urethane leads to a pronounced and dose-dependent reduction of the ability of the bladder to empty during voiding.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that urethane leads to a pronounced and dose-dependent reduction of the ability of the bladder to empty during voiding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Increasing doses of urethane resulted in a gradual decrease in void duration, as quantified by the 20-80% time interval (t20-80).
source: Increasing doses of urethane resulted in a gradual decrease in void duration, as quantified by the 20–80% time interval (t20–80) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Urethane affected the urethral flow rate, showing a gradual decrease at increasing doses.
source: Urethane also affected the urethral flow rate (UFR), which we determined from the time derivative of the changes in bladder volume, showing a gradual decrease at increasing doses (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Incomplete bladder emptying at higher urethane doses is the result of both shorter void duration and reduced flow rate of urine expulsion from the bladder during a void.
source: These findings demonstrate that incomplete bladder emptying at higher urethane doses is the result of both shorter void duration and reduced flow rate of urine expulsion from the bladder during a void.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on void duration and flow rate.

claim: The urethane-induced reduction of urethral flow was the result of a lower urethral flow conductance, while intravesical pressure during a void was not significantly affected.
source: Analysis of the combined intravesical pressure and UFR measurements further revealed that the urethane-induced reduction of urethral flow was the result of a lower urethral flow conductance (UFC), while intravesical pressure during a void was not significantly affected (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from combined pressure and flow measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Urethane has a profound and dose-dependent effect on voiding efficiency, which can be attributed to a reduction in the extent and duration of urethral relaxation.
source: Taken together, these findings reveal that urethane has a profound and dose-dependent effect on voiding efficiency, which can be attributed to a reduction in the extent and duration of urethral relaxation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings on flow conductance and void duration.

claim: There was a dose-dependent decrease in the number of nonvoiding contractions in the 80 s period preceding each void.
source: Moreover, when we analyzed the 80 s period preceding each void, we found a dose-dependent decrease in the number of nonvoiding contractions (Figure 3B and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figures 3B and F.

claim: The impact of surgical catheter implantation on bladder function is poorly understood.
source: In classic cystometry and videocystometry experiments, surgery is performed to implant a catheter into the bladder dome, through which the bladder is filled at a constant, often supraphysiological filling rate. The impact of this invasive intervention on bladder function is poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Injection of a bolus of contrast solution subcutaneously in the scruff region resulted in the excretion of iodine-containing urine, enabling fluoroscopy-based imaging of the bladder without catheter implantation.
source: Injection of a bolus of contrast solution subcutaneously in the scruff region resulted in the excretion of iodine-containing urine, enabling fluoroscopy-based imaging of the bladder without catheter implantation.
evidence: This describes the method developed for non-invasive imaging.

claim: In fluoroscopic volumetry experiments, voids occurred spontaneously at a rate of 1-2 voids per hour during 120 min of imaging.
source: In this setting, the filling rate of the bladder is solely determined by the renal urine output, which we accelerated within a physiologically acceptable range using a diuretic. Animals were imaged during 120 min, during which voids occurred spontaneously at a rate of 1–2 voids per hour, and the machine-learning protocol was used to automatically detect the bladder border.
evidence: This is an observation from the fluoroscopic volumetry experiments.

claim: The average filling rate measured in fluoroscopic volumetry experiments was 7.3 ± 2.8 μl/min.
source: In these experiments, we measured an average filling rate of 7.3 ± 2.8 μl/min (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: Fluoroscopic volumetry allowed for the first time to accurately and continuously quantify volume- and flow-related parameters noninvasively in awake and behaving animals.
source: This approach, fluoroscopic volumetry, allowed for the first time to accurately and continuously quantify volume- and flow-related parameters noninvasively in awake and behaving animals (Figure 4A–C), albeit without concomitant pressure measurement.
evidence: This is stated as a novel capability of the method.

claim: Fluoroscopic volumetry does not provide concomitant pressure measurement.
source: This approach, fluoroscopic volumetry, allowed for the first time to accurately and continuously quantify volume- and flow-related parameters noninvasively in awake and behaving animals (Figure 4A–C), albeit without concomitant pressure measurement.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the fluoroscopic volumetry method.

claim: In noncatheterized animals, bladder capacity amounted to 364 ± 60 µl in the absence of urethane, compared to 89 ± 13 µl in catheterized animals (p = 0.0015).
source: Notably, both in the awake and in the anesthetized conditions, we observed a dramatically larger BC in comparison with catheterized animals: BC amounted to 364 ± 60 µl (compared to 89 ± 13 µl in catheterized animals, p = 0.0015) in the absence of urethane, and to 380 ± 28 µl (compared to 102 ± 18 µl, p = 0.02) after dosing 1.2 g/kg urethane (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In noncatheterized animals, bladder capacity was 380 ± 28 µl after dosing 1.2 g/kg urethane, compared to 102 ± 18 µl in catheterized animals (p = 0.02).
source: Notably, both in the awake and in the anesthetized conditions, we observed a dramatically larger BC in comparison with catheterized animals: BC amounted to 364 ± 60 µl (compared to 89 ± 13 µl in catheterized animals, p = 0.0015) in the absence of urethane, and to 380 ± 28 µl (compared to 102 ± 18 µl, p = 0.02) after dosing 1.2 g/kg urethane (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Complete voiding was detected in awake noncatheterized animals, whereas anesthetized animals had substantial residual volume, corresponding to a voiding efficiency of approximately 60%.
source: Like in the catheterized animals, we detected complete voiding in the awake animals, whereas anesthetized animals had substantial RV, corresponding to a voiding efficiency of ~60% (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluoroscopic volumetry experiments shown in Figures 4E-G.

claim: In comparison with catheterized animals, both the maximal urethral flow rate and the void duration were significantly increased in noncatheterized animals.
source: In comparison with catheterized animals, both the maximal UFR and the void duration were significantly increased (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is a comparative finding shown in Figures 4H-I.

claim: The use of a surgically implanted suprapubic catheter to infuse the mouse bladder has by itself a dramatic effect on bladder function.
source: The above findings indicate that the use of a surgically implanted suprapubic catheter to infuse the mouse bladder has by itself a dramatic effect on bladder function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of catheterized and noncatheterized animals.

claim: The implantation of a catheter into the bladder dome and fixation using a purse-string suture inevitably leads to a reduction of the area of the bladder wall and thus the bladder volume.
source: First, the implantation of a catheter into the bladder dome and fixation using a purse-string suture inevitably leads to a reduction of the area of the bladder wall and thus the bladder volume.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the surgical procedure.

claim: The surface reduction from catheter implantation may only explain a small part (<20%) of the capacity reduction, since the affected surface generally does not exceed 10% of the bladder wall.
source: However, since the affected surface generally does not exceed 10% of the bladder wall, this surface reduction may only explain a small part (<20%) of the capacity reduction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the estimated affected surface area.

claim: The surgical implantation will inevitably induce local bladder irritation and inflammation, which may contribute to the observed reduction in bladder capacity.
source: Second, the surgical implantation will inevitably induce local bladder irritation and inflammation, which may contribute to the observed reduction in BC (Boudes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a potential mechanism with citation support.

claim: Earlier studies have used a 7-day recovery period between surgery and cystometry to reduce the influence of inflammation on bladder function.
source: Whereas we performed our measurements within hours following surgery, earlier studies have used a 7-day recovery period in between surgery and cystometry to reduce the influence of inflammation on bladder function (Yao et al., 2019; Mann-Gow et al., 2017; Cornelissen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to earlier studies.

claim: Studies with a 7-day recovery period report voided volumes in the range of 50-140 μl for adult C57BL/6J mice, similar to values obtained acutely after surgery and substantially lower than the mean voided volume of 380 μl in awake, noncatheterized animals.
source: Notwithstanding the introduction of recovery period, these studies report voided volumes in the range of 50–140 μl for adult C57BL/6J mice (Yao et al., 2019; Mann-Gow et al., 2017; Cornelissen et al., 2008), similar to the values we obtained acutely after surgery, and substantially lower than the mean voided volume of 380 μl in the awake, noncatheterized animals.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature values.

claim: In the fluoroscopic volumetry experiments on furosemide-treated mice, a filling rate of approximately 7 µl/min was measured, which is lower than the 20 μl/min used in videocystometry experiments but higher than the physiological rate of urine production in freely behaving mice of approximately 1-2 µl/min.
source: Lastly, in the fluoroscopic volumetry experiments on furosemide-treated mice we measured a filling rate of ~7 µl/min, which is lower than the 20 μl/min that we used in the videocystometry experiments, but higher than physiological rate of urine production in freely behaving mice of ~1–2 µl/min (Meneton et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured and literature values with citation.

claim: The findings raise an important caveat when interpreting videocystometric results.
source: These findings raise an important caveat when interpreting (video)cystometric results and highlight the usefulness of fluoroscopic volumetry to study bladder function noninvasively, albeit at the expense of intravesical pressure recordings.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: Fluoroscopic volumetry is useful to study bladder function noninvasively, albeit at the expense of intravesical pressure recordings.
source: These findings raise an important caveat when interpreting (video)cystometric results and highlight the usefulness of fluoroscopic volumetry to study bladder function noninvasively, albeit at the expense of intravesical pressure recordings.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the trade-offs of the method.

claim: Experiments were conducted on 12- to 16-week-old female C57BL/6J mice.
source: Experiments were conducted on 12- to 16-week-old female C57BL/6J mice (Janvier).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: All animals were sacrificed after each experiment due to the toxicity associated with urethane anesthesia.
source: After each experiment, all animals were sacrificed due to the toxicity associated with urethane anesthesia.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and ethical considerations.

claim: Videocystometry and suprapubic catheter implantation were performed as described earlier.
source: Videocystometry and suprapubic catheter implantation were performed as described earlier (Franken et al., 2021; Uvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This references previously published methods.

claim: A PE-50 catheter was implanted into the bladder dome of five female mice through an abdominal midline incision while under 2% isoflurane anesthesia.
source: In short, a PE-50 catheter was implanted into the bladder dome of five female mice through an abdominal midline incision while under 2% isoflurane anesthesia (Iso-vet, Dechra veterinary products, Bladel, The Netherlands).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Videocystometry was performed with an infusion of an iodine-based intravesical contrast solution (50% Iomeron 250) at a rate of 20 µl/s.
source: Videocystometry was performed with an infusion of an iodine-based intravesical contrast solution (50% Iomeron 250, Bracco Imaging Europe, Wavre, Belgium) at a rate of 20 µl/s.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Pressure measurements were recorded at 50 Hz, and bladder images were acquired at a frame rate of 30 frames per second.
source: Simultaneously, pressure measurements were recorded at 50 Hz, and bladder images were acquired at a frame rate of 30 frames per second.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Thirty minutes prior to fluoroscopy, mice were injected subcutaneously with the diuretic furosemide (15 mg/kg, 1 mg/ml solution) to increase the diuresis and thereby the filling rate of the bladder.
source: Thirty minutes prior to fluoroscopy, mice were injected subcutaneously with the diuretic furosemide (15 mg/kg, 1 mg/ml solution, Sanofi, Paris, France), to increase the diuresis and thereby the filling rate of the bladder (Monjotin et al., 2017), and with an iodine-containing nonionic radiocontrast agent iodixanol (12 mg I/kg bodyweight, Visipaque 320 mg I/ml; GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol with citation support.

claim: Images were smoothed using a rolling average to enhance image quality for bladder delineation.
source: This image sequence was loaded into NIS Elements-AR 5.30.01 (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan) and smoothed using a rolling average, to enhance image quality for bladder delineation.
evidence: This describes the image processing method.

claim: A rolling average of 15 frames provided an overall suitable image quality with limited influence on key parameters such as the timing and amplitude of the urethral flow rate.
source: Based on simulations using artificial images of an idealized spheroid bladder, we determined that a rolling average of 15 frames provided an overall suitable image quality with limited influence on key parameters such as the timing and amplitude of the UFR (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Segment.ai is an AI module that is part of the NIS-Elements NIS.ai suite, a commercially available (licensed) software.
source: To identify the bladder border in large sets of time-lapse fluoroscopy images, we used Segment.ai, an AI module that is a part of the NIS-Elements NIS.ai suite (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan), a commercially available (licensed) software.
evidence: This describes the software tool used in the study.

claim: The neural network was trained using a set of manually annotated fluoroscopy images in which the contrast-filled bladder was imaged from various angles and at different stages of the filling/voiding cycle.
source: We trained this neural network using a set of manually annotated fluoroscopy images in which the contrast-filled bladder was imaged from various angles and at different stages of the filling/voiding cycle.
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the neural network.

claim: The neural network was repeatedly retrained using images where the bladder was not properly identified until satisfactory identification of the bladder border was achieved in all experiments.
source: It was repeatedly retrained using images where the bladder was not properly identified until satisfactory identification of the bladder border was achieved in all experiments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the iterative training process.

claim: To benchmark the performance of the neural network, 20% of the ground truth annotations were kept aside and used to calculate the Dice similarity index.
source: To benchmark the performance of the neural network, 20% of the ground truth annotations were kept aside, as described in the BIAFLOWS collaborative framework for quality control of object segmentation (Rubens et al., 2020), and used to calculate the DISI
evidence: This describes the validation methodology with citation support.

claim: A Savitzky-Golay digital filter was applied to bladder volume for data smoothing before differentiation to calculate urethral flow rate.
source: From the time course of Vves, we determined a set of parameters related to volume alterations during urine storage and voiding (BC, RV, and Evoiding) and to urine flow during voiding (UFR and UFC), as established earlier (Franken et al., 2021), with an additional Savitzky–Golay digital filter applied to Vves for data smoothing before differentiation to calculate UFR.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: t20-80 represents the interval between the time points at which the bladder volume was reduced by 20% and 80% of the total void volume.
source: As a measure of void duration, we determined t20–80, which represents the interval between the time points at which the bladder volume was reduced by 20% and 80% of the total void volume.
evidence: This defines a parameter used in the analysis.

claim: The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess normality of the data.
source: The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to assess normality of the data.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: A sample size of four to five animals was sufficient to detect a 40% change in key parameters such as voiding efficiency and maximal urethral flow rate with a power of 80% and a significance level of p < 0.05.
source: The sample sizes were calculated based on our earlier work, which yielded that a sample size of four to five animals was sufficient to detect a 40% change in key parameters such as Evoiding and UFRmax with a power of 80% and a significance level of p < 0.05.
evidence: This describes the power analysis for sample size determination.

claim: Urethane suppressed nonvoiding contractions dose-dependently, in line with earlier studies.
source: Urethane did not affect intravesical peak pressure during voiding, but dose-dependently suppressed nonvoiding contractions, in line with earlier studies (Cheng et al., 1995).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to earlier work.

claim: Urethane did not affect intravesical peak pressure during voiding.
source: Urethane did not affect intravesical peak pressure during voiding, but dose-dependently suppressed nonvoiding contractions, in line with earlier studies (Cheng et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The suppressive effect of urethane on voiding cannot be attributed to gradual fatigue of the detrusor muscle in the course of the experiment.
source: As these findings conform to previously published data on bladder volume and voiding efficiency in urethane-anesthetized mice, the suppressive effect of urethane on voiding cannot be attributed to gradual fatigue of the detrusor muscle in the course of the experiment (Franken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: Animals receiving the lowest dose of urethane (0.3 g/kg) were awake and behaving, but displayed a more tranquil behavior than nonanesthetized animals.
source: Throughout these experiments, we observed that animals receiving the lowest dose of urethane (0.3 g/kg) were awake and behaving, but displayed a more tranquil behavior than nonanesthetized animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Both pressure and volume data showed less artifacts in animals treated with 0.3 g/kg urethane.
source: Likewise, both pressure and volume data showed less artifacts in these animals treated with 0.3 g/kg, and there was a trend – albeit not statistically significant – for larger BC, longer ICI, and increased UFR and UFC when compared to nonanesthetized animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: There was a trend for larger bladder capacity, longer intercontractile interval, and increased urethral flow rate and urethral flow conductance at 0.3 g/kg urethane compared to nonanesthetized animals, albeit not statistically significant.
source: Likewise, both pressure and volume data showed less artifacts in these animals treated with 0.3 g/kg, and there was a trend – albeit not statistically significant – for larger BC, longer ICI, and increased UFR and UFC when compared to nonanesthetized animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the statistical analysis.

claim: The analgesia provided by a low dose of urethane (0.3 g/kg) may reduce bladder pain caused by the surgical catheter implantation, thereby improving bladder function.
source: Possibly, the analgesia provided by this low dose of urethane may reduce bladder pain caused by the surgical catheter implantation, thereby improving bladder function.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed trend.

claim: The use of urethane at a dose of 0.3 g/kg may be considered a good compromise between experimental/analytical ease and physiological conditions.
source: Therefore, the use of urethane at a dose of 0.3 g/kg may be considered a good compromise between experimental/analytical ease and physiological conditions.

claim: The implantation of a catheter into the bladder dome and fixation using a purse-string suture generally does not affect more than 10% of the bladder wall surface.
source: However, since the affected surface generally does not exceed 10% of the bladder wall, this surface reduction may only explain a small part (<20%) of the capacity reduction.

claim: The physiological rate of urine production in freely behaving mice is approximately 1-2 µl/min.
source: Lastly, in the fluoroscopic volumetry experiments on furosemide-treated mice we measured a filling rate of ~7 µl/min, which is lower than the 20 μl/min that we used in the videocystometry experiments, but higher than physiological rate of urine production in freely behaving mice of ~1–2 µl/min (Meneton et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Meneton et al., 2000.
